lead: On a curved path, velocity points along the tangent. Acceleration has two perpendicular parts: one changes the speed along the tangent, the other changes the direction toward the centre of curvature. This split explains why a car can keep a steady speed on a bend and still accelerate. Engineers use it for road curves, railway tracks, rotating arms, robot links and satellite paths. The same idea also appears in polar form, where radial and transverse components describe motion measured from a fixed point.
prereq: You need 5.1 for v = ds/dt and Unit 1 for resolving vectors at right angles.

sections.h3: Velocity along the tangent, acceleration in two parts

blocks.text: Take a point P on a curved path. Let s be distance measured along the path from a fixed origin, and let v = ds/dt be the speed in m/s. The velocity vector is always tangent to the path: v = v et, where et is the unit tangent vector. The path also has a unit normal en that points toward the centre of curvature. At P, let ρ (Greek rho, in metres) be the radius of curvature. The acceleration has two perpendicular parts. Tangential acceleration at = dv/dt changes speed. Normal acceleration an = v²/ρ changes direction. Total a = √(at² + an²). Its angle from the tangent is tan⁻¹(an/at), leaning toward the centre. When at = 0 the angle is 90° from the tangent: the acceleration is purely normal, pointing to the centre of curvature. an is never outward. On a circle ρ is constant; on any other curve use ρ at that point. Some syllabi call these intrinsic coordinates or path variables.
a<sub>t</sub> = dv/dt, a<sub>n</sub> = v²/ρ, a = √(a<sub>t</sub>² + a<sub>n</sub>²)
blocks.where: v is speed in m/s; ρ is radius of curvature in m; a<sub>t</sub> and a<sub>n</sub> are acceleration components in m/s².

blocks.text: Use polar coordinates when position is naturally a length and an angle, for example a rotating arm. Let r be distance from the pole in metres and θ the angle in radians. Unit vector er points outward along r; eθ points in the direction of increasing θ. A dot over a symbol means d/dt. The velocity components are vr = ṙ and vθ = rθ̇. The acceleration components are ar = r̈ − rθ̇² and aθ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. Read r̈ as how fast the radial velocity ṙ is changing; −rθ̇² as the inward turning term; 2ṙθ̇ as a term that appears because both radius and angle change. Rectangular components are the special case θ = 0, when ar becomes ẍ and aθ becomes ÿ.

blocks.where: r is distance from the pole in m; θ is angle in rad; each dot is one time derivative; a<sub>r</sub>, a<sub>θ</sub> are in m/s².

figure.caption: The velocity sets the tangent; the acceleration splits into a tangential part that changes speed and a normal part that turns the particle toward the centre of curvature.

spec.title: Acceleration on a curved path
spec.aria: The acceleration of a particle splits into a tangential part that changes its speed and a normal part that turns it toward the centre of curvature; the two add as perpendicular vectors to give the total acceleration. The velocity stays along the tangent.

examples.question: A car enters a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. The driver is still pressing the accelerator, so the speed is rising at 3 m/s². Find the magnitude and direction of the total acceleration at that instant.
steps: Speed v = 20 m/s and radius of curvature ρ = 50 m. Tangential acceleration is given: a_t = dv/dt = 3 m/s² along the tangent.
Normal acceleration: a_n = v²/ρ = 20²/50 = 400/50 = 8 m/s², directed toward the centre.
Direction: angle from tangent = tan⁻¹(a_n/a_t) = tan⁻¹(8/3) = 69.4°, toward the centre of curvature.
examples.answer: The total acceleration is 8.54 m/s² at 69.4° from the tangent toward the centre of curvature.
examples.check:
import math
v = 20.0
rho = 50.0
at = 3.0
an = v**2 / rho
a = math.hypot(at, an)
angle = math.degrees(math.atan2(an, at))
print(round(an, 2))
print(at)
print(round(a, 2))
print(round(angle, 1))

traps: Using a_n = v²/r only for circles: on any curved path use the radius of curvature ρ at that point.
Pointing a_n away from the centre: normal acceleration always points toward the centre of curvature.
Adding a_t and a_n as ordinary numbers: they are perpendicular, so use √(a_t² + a_n²).
In polar form, dropping −rθ̇² or 2ṙθ̇, or using degrees instead of radians for θ̇ and θ̈.
Calling a_t the total acceleration: a_t changes only speed; the total includes the direction-changing part.

quiz.q: Write the formulas for a_t and a_n on a curved path.
quiz.a: a_t = dv/dt and a_n = v²/ρ, where v is speed and ρ is radius of curvature.

quiz.q: Why does velocity have no component normal to the path?
quiz.a: Velocity is the rate of change of position along the path. At an instant, motion is along the tangent, so its normal component is zero.

quiz.q: A particle moves on a circle of radius 4 m at constant speed 12 m/s. Find its acceleration.
quiz.a: a_t = 0 because speed is constant. a_n = 12²/4 = 144/4 = 36 m/s² toward the centre.

quiz.q: For polar motion, r = 3 m, ṙ = 2 m/s, r̈ = 1 m/s², θ̇ = 0.5 rad/s, θ̈ = 0. Find a_r and a_θ.
A car goes around a bend at constant speed. Is its acceleration zero? Explain.
quiz.a: No. a_t = 0 because speed is constant, but direction changes, so a_n = v²/ρ is nonzero and points toward the centre.

quiz.q: What does the radius of curvature ρ mean at a point on a path?
quiz.a: It is the radius of the circle that best matches the curve at that point.

quiz.q: A car brakes while turning left. Give the directions of a_t and a_n.
quiz.a: a_t points opposite the velocity because speed is decreasing; a_n points toward the centre of the left turn.

beyond: Not for the exam. Road designers use these components to set safe banking and speed limits on curves. Vehicle stability systems compare measured yaw and acceleration with a_n = v²/ρ to detect skids. Robotics uses radial-transverse terms for rotating arms and tangential-normal terms for tool paths. Search next for intrinsic coordinates, radius of curvature, and centripetal acceleration in vehicle dynamics.
